newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: UNION MEMBERS TO MEET ON PUBLIC SERVICE IR PLANS
The Community and Public Sector Union will hold talks with members this week to decide on a response to Federal Government plans to remove equal award conditions for public servants.
Industrial Relations Minister, Peter Reith, told unions last night the government has instructed managers to offer its 130,000 public servants individual contracts.
Under new industrial relations legislation which comes into force this month, different working conditions will be negotiated for each department.
The CPSU's Doug Lilley, says industrial action will be inevitable if the new arrangements are pushed through.
TOP LEVEL MEETING ON NSW TEACHERS

The New South Wales Premier is chairing a top level meeting into allegations that more than 100 teachers with a history of child sexual abuse allegations levelled against them remain employed in the state's education system.
The claims have been made before the NSW Police Royal Commission.
Premier Bob Carr is under presssure to immediately suspend the teachers.
An hour ago he began a meeting to decide the immediate future of the teachers, which involved senior ministers and bureaucrats.
Among those present are Police Minister Paul Whelan and his commissioner Peter Ryan along with Attorney General Jeff Shaw.
The Education Department Director General Ken Boston is also in attendance.
APPEAL FOR TRANSPORT WORKERS NOT TO STRIKE
Victorian Premier, Jeff Kennett, has appealed to public transport workers who are threatening strike action which would disrupt this weekend's Grand Prix in Melbourne.
Mr Kennett says such action would be a "kick in the guts" for race fans, and could harm the city's 2006 Commmonwealth Games bid.
Members of the Public Transport Union are holding stopwork meetings this morning to decide their next move.
A strike on Saturday and Sunday would leave private buses and taxis the only transport to the Grand prix.
REPORT ON NT'S VOLUNTARY EUTHANASIA LAW TABLED
The Senate report into the Northern Territory's voluntary euthanasia law has been tabled in the Federal senate.
It's understood the report contains no recommendations, because the ultimate vote on the Andrews anti-voluntary euthanasia bill will be one of conscience.
Territory Senator Grant Tambling has already responded to the report, calling it unrepresentative and deficient.

Senator Tambling and Senator Bob Collins have added their own comments to the document, saying it doesn't sufficiently acknowlege the impact the Andrews bill could have on the legal and constitutional future of the Territory.
LEADERS LIKELY TO LOOK AT DUMPING BANK ACCOUNT TAX
A plan to dump one of the taxes on "everyday" bank accounts is expected to be put to State and Territory leaders at their meeting in Melbourne tomorrow.
The proposal to get rid of the Financial Institutions Duty has been floated over a number of years, but changing technology and a new political climate are giving it renewed impetus.
The FID raises hundreds of millions of dollars a year in States' revenue.
If agreement on its abolition is reached, it would be compensated for by a broadening of the Debits Tax, which now only applies to cheque linked accounts.
SENTENCING FOR MAN WHO BURNT SCHOOL BOY
The Supreme Court in Cairns will this morning hand down the sentence against the man found guilty of attempting to murder schoolboy, Tjandamurra O'Shane.
Paul Wade Streeton was yesterday found guilty of attempted murder and griveous bodily harm with intent.
Streeton poured petrol over the six-year-old boy and set him alight as he played in his Cairns North Primary School playground last October.
Tjandamurra received burns to 70 per cent of his body in the attack.
His family is calling for life imprisonment for 27-year-old Streeton.
WA HEP-C CHECKS FIND MORE THAN HALF POSITIVE
More than half of the people tested for Hepatitis-C after being recalled by the West Australian Health department, have been diagnosed with the disease.
Earlier this month the Health Department wrote to 187 people who received blood transfusions between 1970 and 1990, before donor screening was in place, asking them to undergo testing.
Communicable disease specialist, Lewis Marshall, says of the 24 tested so far, 14 people have Hepatitis-C.
He's urging anyone who received a letter to come forward to ensure their own status, and to ensure the safety of those in close contact with them.
